##### DATASET DESCRIPTION #####

### DATASETS: ###

Dataset Name: reef.csv
Dataset Description: Each reef is surveyed once per year by a team of divers using stratified belt transects. Surveys include four transects (replicates) per depth stratum. Most reefs have two strata, although some have only one. Reefs are nested within regions, and each transect area recorded in the dataset should total 250 square meters. # Fish Productivity Dynamics on Rocky Reefs: Rocky reef ecosystems sustain surprisingly high fish productivity despite often occurring in nutrient-poor tropical or subtropical waters (Morais and Bellwood 2019). Fish biomass production (the rate at which fish community biomass is generated through growth and reproduction) can be decoupled from the standing biomass(Morais and Bellwood 2020; Morais, Connolly, and Bellwood 2020; Graham et al. 2017). In other words, having more fish biomass on a reef does not always mean proportionally higher productivity. This is because productivity depends on energy flux and turnover rates: small, fast-growing fish can rapidly generate biomass, whereas larger, slow-growing species turn over more slowly (Morais, Connolly, and Bellwood 2020). For example, heavy fishing pressure tends to remove large, long-lived fishes, but the remaining community of smaller fish can exhibit a higher production per unit biomass (through faster growth and reproduction) – a compensatory effect that buffers total fish production even as biomass declines (Morais, Connolly, and Bellwood 2020). Morais and Bellwood (2020) refer to this as “buffering productivity”, warning that one cannot assume resource production is directly equivalent to standing biomass (Morais, Connolly, and Bellwood 2020). This insight is as research on productivity should account for community size structure and life histories, not just total biomass. On coral and rocky reefs, multiple trophic pathways contribute to fish productivity. Herbivorous fishes convert algal and detrital production into fish biomass, planktivorous fishes capture pelagic energy subsidies, and higher trophic levels redistribute this production via predation (Morais and Bellwood 2019). Notably, pelagic subsidies (offshore plankton and nutrients transported onto reefs) can underpin fish productivity in degraded reefs where benthic production is low. Morais and Bellwood (2019) documented a reef with only ~6% live coral cover (after mass coral mortality) that nevertheless maintained high fish production by virtue of planktivorous fish feeding on pelagic zooplankton (Morais and Bellwood 2019; Morais et al. 2021). These planktivores had relatively small standing biomass but high turnover, so their contribution to production would be missed if one looked only at biomass(Morais and Bellwood 2019; Morais et al. 2021). This finding emphasizes that reef fish communities are tightly linked to surrounding oceanographic productivity. In the Gulf of California, rocky reefs benefit from episodic upwelling and plankton-rich currents, suggesting that pelagic input may similarly enhance local fish production. Energy fluxes on Gulf reefs likely involve strong benthic-pelagic coupling: reef fishes capitalize on both benthic invertebrates/algae and pelagic prey, resulting in high secondary production in an otherwise oligotrophic region. A significant portion of reef fish productivity comes from the smallest, often overlooked components of the community. Cryptobenthic fishes – tiny, short-lived species like gobies and blennies – have extremely rapid population turnover. Recent studies estimate that cryptobenthic fishes contribute only on the order of 13–20% of the net fish biomass production on reefs, yet they account for ~60% of the fish biomass consumed by predators (Brandl et al. 2019). In essence, these miniature fishes are produced and eaten so quickly that they fuel a large fraction of the reef’s energy flow to higher trophic levels (Brandl et al. 2019). Such pathways are invisible if we only track standing stocks. This implies that production-to-biomass (P/B) ratios can be very high for certain functional groups (planktivores, small cryptobenthics) and lower for others (large predators). Theoretical expectations from metabolic theory (scaling of production with body size and temperature) can inform these: smaller-bodied reef fish (or communities in warmer waters) will have higher P/B ratios, reflecting faster turnover, whereas larger-bodied or cooler-water communities will have lower P/B. Empirically, benchmarks from tropical reefs indicate overall fish production on healthy reefs can range roughly in the order of 1–4 tons of fish biomass produced per hectare per year, with variability driven by community composition and productivity regimes (Aburto-Oropeza et al. 2011) . For instance, the Cabo Pulmo no-take reserve in the southern Gulf of California saw its fish biomass increase to ~4.24 t/ha over a decade of protection (a 463% rise), suggesting a high underlying productivity that was realized once fishing ceased (Aburto-Oropeza et al. 2011). Such values provide a ballpark for upper-end productivity in productive reef systems, which can guide novel hypothesis for models of fish stock dynamics in the region. # Species Diversity and Turnover Patterns: Reef fish communities are dynamic in space and time, showing variations in both alpha diversity (local species richness) and beta diversity (compositional turnover among sites or times). In relatively pristine conditions, alpha diversity on Gulf of California rocky reefs is moderate – typically tens of fish species per site, lower than coral triangle reefs but still ecologically rich. Beta diversity in the Gulf has historically been high due to strong environmental gradients: the Gulf spans subtropical to warm-temperate conditions, creating distinct northern vs. southern assemblages. An oceanographic and thermal boundary in the mid-Gulf has long separated cooler-water communities in the north from more tropical communities in the south. However, climate change is driving shifts in these patterns. Recent monitoring shows that this ecological boundary has moved northward by ~1.5° latitude over the past decade as waters warm (Favoretto, Sánchez, and Aburto-Oropeza 2022). In effect, formerly distinct communities are becoming more similar (tropicalization of the north), thus homogenizing community composition across the Gulf (Favoretto, Sánchez, and Aburto-Oropeza 2022). From a modeling perspective, this suggests that priors on species occupancy or turnover should allow for non-stationarity: spatial community differences may diminish under warming scenarios. Climate-driven species turnover is evident in many reef systems globally. Gradual ocean warming and especially extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs) can cause rapid reorganization of fish communities (Favoretto, Sánchez, and Aburto-Oropeza 2022; Ziegler et al. 2023) . Warm-affinity species extend their ranges or increase in dominance, while cool-affinity species retreat or disappear – a process termed “tropicalization.” In Western Australia, for example, an anomalous warming event led to the collapse of kelp forests and their replacement by turf algae and herbivorous tropical fishes, fundamentally shifting the community to one dominated by warm-water species. In the Gulf of California, warming trends are likewise altering fish assemblages. Over roughly 20 years, average sea temperatures in parts of the Gulf rose by up to 3 °C, and surveys at remote Isla San José (mid-Gulf) recorded a ~40% drop in fish genus richness compared to 2001. Many previously resident species were absent by 2024–2025, indicating local extirpations or shifts in distribution, even as the total number of individual fish observed per survey increased. In other words, fewer species are now making up the bulk of the community – a sign of simplification of diversity. This kind of turnover (loss of diversity with compensation by a few tolerant species) is an important empirical benchmark for climate impacts. It introduces uncertainties in ecosystem function, as a less diverse community may be less resilient. When formulating novel hypothesis here, one might expect higher variance in species composition year-to-year under current warming trends, and possibly include parameters for increased dominance by warm-water generalists at the expense of specialists. Even short-term events can produce marked community turnover. The 2014–2016 Pacific warm anomaly (“the Blob”) and a strong El Niño struck the Gulf and Baja region, providing a natural experiment. Observations at both protected and fished sites in the southern California Current (just north of the Gulf) revealed taxonomic diversity declines and shifts in trophic structure after the heatwave (Ziegler et al. 2023) . Notably, research found that while all sites saw an initial drop in species richness and a reordering of which trophic groups were present, marine reserves (MPAs) had some buffering capacity: inside MPAs, the loss of functional (trophic) diversity was dampened and species richness recovered about 75% faster over the following four years compared to fished sites (Ziegler et al. 2023). This suggests that intact, large populations and diverse food webs within MPAs can confer resilience – an important consideration for turnover rates in models. With protection, communities might bounce back to prior compositions more readily (higher community stability), whereas heavily exploited systems might undergo more permanent regime shifts after disturbances. Therefore, temporal turnover could be conditioned on management or exploitation status, anticipating more stability (lower turnover) in less disturbed reefs. At larger scales, beta diversity patterns on reefs indicate that many functions and lineages are regionally restricted, meaning species turnover across geography is high in reef fish (each region or reef has a somewhat unique assemblage). This is relevant as one should expect significant spatial random effects or variation in community composition. However, as warming proceeds, one hypothesis (supported by early evidence in the Gulf (Favoretto, Sánchez, and Aburto-Oropeza 2022) ) is a biogeographic homogenization – tropical generalist species expanding range and making distant reef communities more alike. Such homogenization would reduce beta diversity over time. This process is uncertain and may be nonlinear, as some species cannot disperse equally or habitat differences may still maintain uniqueness. # Functional Traits, Roles, and Redundancy in Reef Fish Communities: Reef fish assemblages perform a variety of functional roles (e.g. grazing algae, predation on urchins or fish, planktivory, bioerosion of reef structure), and the distribution of functional traits among species is a key determinant of ecosystem resilience. A recurring theme in reef ecology is the degree of functional redundancy – whether multiple species fulfill similar roles such that losing one species can be compensated by others. Earlier assumptions held that high species richness would ensure redundancy, acting as “insurance” for ecosystem function. However, both theoretical and global empirical analyses have challenged this notion. Even in species-rich coral reef systems, many functions are in fact supported by only one or a few species, making those functions inherently vulnerable to species losses(Mouillot et al. 2014). Mouillot et al. (2014) found that reef fish faunas tend to be over-redundant in a few common functions (many species crowding into similar roles), but highly vulnerable in others (unique functions carried out by single species). In their global analysis, a substantial fraction of functional entities (unique trait combinations) had only one species representing them, meaning the extinction of that species would eliminate the function entirely. This result has been echoed by earlier work in specific regions: Bellwood, Hughes, and others noted “limited functional redundancy” on coral reefs, where surprisingly few species of herbivorous fishes were critical for controlling algae and maintaining coral habitat(Morais, Connolly, and Bellwood 2020) . In practical terms, for the Gulf of California’s rocky reefs – which have lower total fish diversity than Indo-Pacific coral reefs – functional redundancy is likely even more constrained. Many functional groups (for instance, large herbivorous parrotfishes, or certain apex predators) are represented by just one or a handful of species in the Gulf. This implies that for functional trait coverage should allow for strong sensitivity: the removal or decline of a single species can cause a noticeable drop in functional diversity. Functional trait distributions (body sizes, diets, mobility, thermal tolerance, etc.) influence how reef fish communities respond to environmental change. Traits confer both resistance and recovery potential. For example, smaller opportunistic feeders might increase in abundance if large competitors or predators are removed (as seen when fishing down food webs releases lower-trophic-level fishes (Sala et al. 2004)). Conversely, species with certain traits (e.g. dependency on corals or cooler water) may be the first to decline as habitats degrade or temperatures rise. In the Gulf of California, one documented pattern is that warming has favored fish species with more tropical affinities and often generalized feeding habits, whereas more specialized or cooler-water associated species have dwindled (Favoretto, Sánchez, and Aburto-Oropeza 2022) . Additionally, some functions may amplify or dampen climate impacts: herbivorous fish traits, for instance, could either mitigate climate effects by preventing algal overgrowth after coral mortality (thus facilitating coral recovery), or if lost due to fishing, could exacerbate reef degradation. Functional redundancy among herbivores is a particular focus in reef resilience theory. If multiple grazing species are present, algal blooms can be controlled even if one grazer declines; but if only one grazer species exists and it is overfished or climate-stressed, algal overgrowth could occur, hindering coral and rocky reef invertebrate recruitment. Indeed, studies have shown that reefs with intact guilds of herbivores and predators can better resist phase shifts under stress (Ziegler et al. 2023) , whereas those already missing key functional players may undergo rapid change. In terms of empirical benchmarks, functional diversity on reefs does not scale linearly with species diversity. Remarkably, adding more species beyond a certain point yields diminishing returns in new functions – a dozen well-chosen species can cover a large fraction of possible functional space (Mouillot et al. 2014). However, the vulnerability of that functional space remains high if those species are rare or environmentally sensitive (Mouillot et al. 2014). In the Gulf, some functional groups (e.g. planktivorous damselfish, small cryptobenthics) are abundant and continuously replenish, whereas others (e.g. large predatory groupers or endemic butterflyfish that depend on specific prey) are inherently scarce. This mismatch means functional redundancy is uneven: production-related roles (energy turnover through small fish) might be robust, but certain biogenic or top-down control roles could be one species away from collapse. A clear example emerged from a Gulf of California marine reserve study: despite a general increase in fish biomass over time inside the reserve, both species richness and functional richness actually declined (Ramírez-Ortiz et al. 2020) . The loss of functional richness implies that some roles were lost or diminished even as total fish amount grew. This paradox may be explained by climate-driven losses of certain functionally unique species that protection alone could not safeguard (e.g. species at their thermal limits), combined with a few warm-tolerant, generalist species booming in number and biomass. For modeling purposes, this underscores the need to treat functional diversity and biomass trends as separate priors – a community could become quantitatively more productive (more biomass) but qualitatively less diverse in traits, which could portend longer-term instability. Uncertainty in trait-based responses should be incorporated, perhaps via scenario that reflect different degrees of functional compensation vs. functional loss under stress. # Environmental and Anthropogenic Drivers: The structure and productivity of Gulf of California rocky reef communities are shaped by both environmental conditions and human impacts. Climate change – particularly ocean warming – has emerged as a dominant driver of ecological change on reefs. Over the last few decades, average sea surface temperatures in the Gulf have risen significantly, and extreme warm events have become roughly three times more frequent than in the late 20th century. This chronic warming and increase in heatwaves leads to physiological stress on many species, altered reproduction and recruitment patterns, and changing interspecies interactions. The recent warming has already caused measurable declines in fish biomass (e.g. a 43% decrease in overall reef fish biomass was documented in one long-term study coinciding with the warm 2010–2020 period (Favoretto, Sánchez, and Aburto-Oropeza 2022) ) and shifts in community composition toward warm-water species as discussed. From a broad literature perspective, marine heatwaves are especially damaging: modeling predicts that short-term heatwaves can drive biomass losses and range shifts several times faster than gradual warming alone (Ziegler et al. 2023) . Empirical observations bear this out – mass mortality of temperature-sensitive species, collapse of habitat-forming organisms (like corals or kelps), and “community tropicalization” have been recorded after heatwave events in multiple regions (Ziegler et al. 2023). For the Gulf, this means our hypothesis related to climate drivers should allow for sudden, step-like changes in key parameters (e.g. sudden drops in diversity or biomass corresponding to heatwave years) rather than only smooth trends. Another critical driver is fishing pressure and its management (or lack thereof). Reefs in the Gulf of California have been subject to intense exploitation for decades, which has altered fish community structure and function. Sala et al. (2004) provided stark evidence of “fishing down the food web” in the Gulf: over 30 years, fisheries shifted from targeting large, long-lived, top-trophic predators to increasingly focusing on smaller, lower-trophic species as the larger ones became depleted (Sala et al. 2004). The average maximum size of fish in landings shrank by ~45 cm in just 20 years (Sala et al. 2004). This size-selective overfishing not only reduced populations of groupers, sharks, and other apex predators, but also cascaded through the ecosystem – smaller prey fish populations initially increased (due to release from predation) until they too were heavily fished, and overall community trophic structure simplified. Catch-per-unit-effort data showed declines for most species groups after the early 1980s, despite increased fishing effort, indicating unsustainable extraction (Sala et al. 2004). These historical data inform prior expectations: we expect lower standing biomass and truncated size distributions on heavily fished reefs, as well as potentially elevated production-to-biomass ratios (since the community is skewed toward fast-growing small fishes, as noted earlier (Morais, Connolly, and Bellwood 2020; Graham et al. 2017) ). We also anticipate certain functions (e.g. predation by large carnivores) to be underrepresented on fished reefs. Conversely, where fishing is reduced or stopped, significant recoveries can occur. The Cabo Pulmo reserve’s 463% biomass increase over 10 years (including a >10-fold rebound of top predators) stands as a global exemplar of reef recovery (Aburto-Oropeza et al. 2011) . Similarly, other no-take areas in the Gulf have shown greater resilience to climate perturbations, as mentioned with faster post-heatwave recovery of diversity inside MPAs. These cases suggest that fishing pressure and climate stress can interact: overfishing may exacerbate climate impacts by removing species that would otherwise confer resilience (e.g. herbivores that prevent algal overgrowth, or predators that control boom-bust prey dynamics). Potential analysis to test novel hypothesis could incorporate interaction terms or conditional effects where high fishing pressure prior leads to larger climate-induced changes in community metrics. Habitat degradation is another driver tied to both climate and local stressors. In coral reef contexts, loss of live coral cover (from coral bleaching, disease, or physical destruction) reduces structural complexity and the resources for coral-associated fishes, often causing declines in coral-specialist fish and overall reef fish diversity. The rocky reefs of the Gulf of California are not as coral-dominated as Indo-Pacific reefs, but they do host corals (e.g. Pocillopora spp. in some sites) and a rich benthic invertebrate community that provides food and shelter for fish. Warming-related coral mortality has been observed in the southern Gulf during strong El Niño events, and such events can shift fish communities toward those favoring non-coral habitat. For instance, Favoretto et al. (2022) noted that after recent El Niño warming, stony coral species with warm-water affinities became more common, while cooler-water coral species declined, which in turn likely affected the fish assemblages tied to those corals. Additionally, anthropogenic habitat impacts like coastal development or pollution are present but localized in the Gulf (e.g. sedimentation near ports, disturbances from tourism in popular reef sites). Overall, environmental drivers (temperature, storms, nutrients) and human drivers (fishing, pollution) create a complex disturbance regime. Known patterns include: seasonal upwelling in the Gulf’s midriff region boosting productivity, occasional hypoxia in the northern Gulf affecting benthic communities, and cyclical climate oscillations (Pacific Decadal Oscillation, ENSO) affecting recruitment success of various fish cohorts. Hypothesis that reflect environmental variability – for example, higher uncertainty in recruitment or biomass growth parameters in years of extreme conditions – are warranted. It is also important to highlight uncertainties and emerging trends. One uncertainty is how permanent or reversible climate-driven changes will be. The “tropicalization” of the Gulf’s rocky reefs is underway, but its long-term consequences remain unclear. Some models predict potential new community equilibriums; others suggest continual flux if species migrations keep pace with warming. Another uncertainty lies in threshold effects: e.g. if a critical functional group (like a key grazer or predator) falls below a threshold, the system could tip into a different state (algal-dominated, or dominated by a few planktivores, etc.). These possibilities mean that prior distributions might need fat tails or multi-modal structures to allow for the probability of regime shifts. The literature provides empirical benchmarks for some thresholds (such as a minimum herbivorous fish biomass needed to prevent runaway algal growth, or a minimum predator biomass to keep mesopredator prey in check), though these are context-specific. # Patterns and Anomalies in Gulf of California Rocky Reefs: The Gulf of California’s rocky reefs exhibit several notable patterns, some of which distinguish them from other reef systems and some that serve as microcosms of global processes. One hallmark is the high productivity and biomass potential of Gulf reefs despite moderate species richness. The Gulf is often called the “Aquarium of the World” for its rich marine life; indeed, this region produces roughly 50% of Mexico’s fisheries yield, underscoring how productive its waters are. Nutrient upwelling and a semi-enclosed sea effect make parts of the Gulf extremely fertile, supporting dense schools of planktivorous fish and swift energy transfer to higher trophic levels. Consequently, rocky reefs here can accumulate substantial fish biomass (as seen in protected sites like Cabo Pulmo) and support robust fisheries. This is somewhat anomalous when compared to many nutrient-poor coral atolls. One might set higher baseline expectations for productivity or carrying capacity in the Gulf relative to an average tropical reef, acknowledging this productive backdrop. Another pattern is the pronounced biogeographic gradient along the Gulf’s length. The northern Gulf’s rocky reefs (e.g. near the Midriff Islands or Bahía de los Ángeles) historically harbored a mix of temperate and subtropical species – including large Gulf grouper (Mycteroperca jordani), broomtail grouper (Mycteroperca xenarcha), and endemic basses – adapted to cooler, fluctuating conditions. The southern Gulf (near La Paz and Cabo Pulmo) hosts more typically tropical assemblages – e.g. various parrotfish, surgeonfish, butterflyfish, and smaller reef sharks – akin to those in the adjacent Pacific south of Baja. Between these, an ecological transition zone around ~28–29°N has been documented, corresponding to oceanographic discontinuities (currents, temperature, and nutrient differences) (Favoretto et al., 2022). This spatial turnover means that species beta diversity within the Gulf is quite high – a reef fish survey in the Midriff islands will yield a different species list than one in the Cape region. However, as mentioned, warming is shifting this. The recent northward shift of warm conditions has effectively eroded some of the north-south differences, leading to more tropical species appearing farther north and some cooler-water species retreating. An example is the increased observations of surgeonfishes and pufferfishes around islands where they were previously rare, coupled with declines in bass and sculpin-like species that prefer cooler water (as noted anecdotally by local fishers and studies like the Isla San José comparison). This suggests that location (latitude within the Gulf) is a less static predictor of community composition than it used to be – temporal trends need to be included. Community turnover in the Gulf also includes some peculiar cases. One such anomaly was observed in the Espíritu Santo National Park (adjacent to La Paz) over a decade of protection: while the no-take MPA successfully increased total fish biomass and maintained stable densities, researchers found a decrease in local fish diversity and functional richness over the same period (Ramírez-Ortiz et al. 2020) . Fewer species and functions were present, even though the reef had more fish by weight than before. This counterintuitive result likely reflects the interplay of protection with external stressors. Inside the reserve, a few species (for example, mid-level predators or hardy omnivores) may have proliferated and dominated biomass, while climate stress eliminated some less common, functionally unique species – a combination yielding higher biomass but lower diversity. It serves as a cautionary tale that marine protected areas, while crucial, cannot by themselves offset all impacts of climate change or other broad-scale pressures. For hypotheses, it means one should allow for scenarios where biomass-based metrics improve but diversity-based metrics deteriorate. It also highlights uncertainty in how community metrics correlate: high biomass doesn’t always equate to high diversity or balanced function, especially under rapid environmental change. Another notable pattern in the Gulf’s rocky reefs is the role of functional groups under different conditions. For instance, herbivorous fishes (parrotfishes, damselfishes, chubs) are present but not as diverse as in coral-rich regions. In the northern Gulf, much of the grazing pressure historically came from sea urchins rather than fish, whereas in the southern Gulf, herbivorous fish play a larger role. This means the Gulf’s resilience to coral-algae phase shifts might differ from a typical coral reef – macroalgae can proliferate if both urchins (sensitive to El Niño warming) and herbivorous fish (sensitive to fishing) are reduced. There have been reports of localized algal overgrowth in some degraded Gulf reefs, but also cases where herbivore populations (e.g. monospecific schools of Kyphosus chubs or Siganus rabbitfish, an introduced species in the southern Gulf) kept algal cover in check. We thus see functional compensation in some areas (non-native or unusual herbivores taking on roles) which adds complexity. Including the possibility of such compensatory dynamics (e.g. a non-native species filling a vacant niche, or an invertebrate grazer compensating for fish loss) might be beyond the scope of a simple prior, but qualitatively it is an uncertainty to acknowledge. In summary, the Gulf of California’s rocky reef ecology is characterized by high productivity fueled by oceanographic subsidies, a gradient of community composition that is now shifting due to warming, and a delicate balance of functional roles that can be upset by exploitation or climate disturbances. The literature – from Morais and Bellwood’s work on reef fish production to regional studies on Gulf community changes – suggests a set of theoretical expectations: namely, that fish production can remain surprisingly resilient (up to a point) even as biomass or diversity changes, that species turnover will accelerate under climate warming (with a trend toward homogenization by warm-adapted species), that functional redundancy is limited such that certain losses have outsized impacts, and that local human pressures (fishing) can either undermine or, if managed (MPAs), bolster the reef’s ability to cope with climate stress. Empirical benchmarks like the ~4 t/ha fish biomass in unfished Gulf reefs (Favoretto et al. 2024; Aburto-Oropeza et al. 2011) , the 40% loss of fish diversity in two decades at a warming site, or the 60% contribution of tiny cryptobenthic fish to predator diets can all inform prior distributions for model parameters (e.g. carrying capacity, species turnover rates, interaction strengths). Finally, uncertainties remain high regarding the long-term outcome of climate changes – whether gradual adaptation or sudden tipping points will occur – and these uncertainties should be reflected in suitably broad or flexible. The Gulf of California, with its fast-changing yet highly productive reefs, offers both cautionary and optimistic case studies for how reef ecosystems might respond to the confluence of global and local pressures.

### COLUMNS: ###

year:
  Calendar year when the survey took place. Monitoring is conducted annually, although not every reef was visited every year. Type: dbl. Levels: 1998-2024.

month:
  Calendar month of the survey. Most monitoring occurred between August and December, with occasional observations from other months. Type: dbl. Levels: 2-12.

day:
  Calendar day of the survey. Type: dbl. Levels: 1-31.

region:
  Region in Baja California where the survey occurred. For spatial analyses, the 'degree' column provides broader latitudinal groupings. Type: chr. Levels: La Paz, Corredor, Loreto, Cabo Pulmo, La Ventana, Alto Golfo, San Basilio.

id_reef:
  Numeric code assigned to each reef. Type: dbl. Levels: 1-448.

reef:
  Reef name. Type: chr. Levels: -.

degree:
  Latitudinal degree of the survey location, derived from the latitude column. Type: dbl. Levels: 23-30.

longitude:
  Longitude (WGS84) of the reef's GPS location. Type: dbl. Levels: Min: -113.6 to -109.4.

latitude:
  Latitude (WGS84) of the reef's GPS location. Type: dbl. Levels: Min: 23.32 to 29.56.

depth:
  Depth stratum of each transect (Shallow = 5 m, Deep = 20 m). Type: chr. Levels: Shallow, Deep.

mpa:
  Name of the Marine Protected Area (MPA) containing the reef; NA indicates sites outside protected polygons. Type: chr. Levels: -.

protection_status:
  Protection level of each reef. 'Cabo Pulmo' denotes the strictest protection, 'weak regulations' indicates limited enforcement, 'sin proteccion' indicates no protection, and NA indicates sites outside assessed protection. Type: chr. Levels: cabo pulmo, weak regulations, sin proteccion, NA.

transect:
  Unique identifier for each transect within a reef. Type: dbl. Levels: -.

area:
  Area (square meters) surveyed per transect. Some transects may cover less than 250 m² due to logistical constraints. Type: dbl. Levels: 250.

trophic_level:
  Trophic level of each fish species, indicating its position within the food web. Type: dbl. Levels: 2-4.5.

genus:
  Scientific genus of the species. Type: chr. Levels: -.

species:
  Scientific species name (genus and species). Type: chr. Levels: -.

quantity:
  Number of individuals in a given species-size class observed within a transect. Type: dbl. Levels: 1-4500.

size:
  Estimated total length of individuals (centimeters). Type: dbl. Levels: 5-180.

biomass:
  Biomass calculated from von Bertalanffy growth parameters, size, and quantity, expressed in ton/ha (tons per hectare). Type: dbl. Levels: 0.000024-85.78.

prod:
  Estimated productivity derived from biomass, temperature, and additional growth parameters, including mortality. Type: dbl. Levels: 0.03-3803.

turnover:
  Biomass turnover rate for the species-size class, indicating how quickly biomass is replenished. Type: dbl. Levels: 0.01-28.6.

mean_sst:
  Annual mean sea surface temperature for the reef, derived from remote sensing. Type: dbl. Levels: 21.2-26.59.

mean_chla:
  Annual mean chlorophyll-a concentration for the reef, derived from remote sensing. Type: dbl. Levels: 0.25-6.7.

PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: The productivity-to-biomass ratio (P/B) declines with increasing latitude (degree) after accounting for local mean sea surface temperature (mean_sst).

Experiment objective: Quantify the relationship between latitude and P/B ratio while controlling for mean SST to test if cooler waters at higher latitudes yield lower turnover per unit biomass.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Compute P/B ratio for each transect observation as prod/biomass.  
2. Exclude observations with zero biomass to avoid division errors.  
3. Aggregate by reef-year-depth to compute mean P/B, mean degree, and mean_sst across transects.  
4. Fit a linear mixed‐effects model (e.g., using statsmodels or lme4) with mean P/B as response, degree and mean_sst as fixed effects, and random intercepts for region or id_reef.  
5. Assess the significance and sign of the degree coefficient while inspecting collinearity with mean_sst.  
6. Validate assumptions via residual diagnostics and, if needed, include quadratic terms or splines for degree.

Deliverables:
1. Table of model coefficients with confidence intervals.  
2. Diagnostic plots (residuals vs fitted, Q-Q plot).  
3. Scatterplot of P/B vs degree colored by mean_sst with fitted regression line.

Analysis:
The code successfully computed a per‐transect P/B ratio, aggregated it by reef‐year‐depth, and fitted a linear mixed‐effects model with region as a random intercept. Variance Inflation Factors (VIF ≈2.76 for both degree and mean SST) indicate low collinearity. The fixed‐effects estimate for latitude (mean_degree) is negative (–1116) but its 95% CI (–6196 to 3964) overlaps zero, showing no significant decline of P/B with latitude after accounting for SST. The SST effect is positive (2689) with a CI (10 to 5369) that excludes zero, indicating warmer reefs have higher P/B. Residual diagnostics show no obvious heteroscedasticity but some heavy tails in the residual distribution. The scatterplot of mean P/B vs latitude (colored by SST) with the fitted line at mean SST (~24.6 °C) corroborates these findings: there’s no clear latitudinal gradient in P/B once SST is included. Overall, the hypothesis that P/B declines with latitude—after controlling for SST—is not supported by this model.

Hypothesis: After controlling for biomass density, deep transects (20 m) exhibit higher biomass turnover rates than shallow transects (5 m).

Experiment objective: Quantify the effect of depth stratum on biomass turnover, accounting for biomass.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Use transect‐level data: extract turnover and biomass values. 2. Encode depth as a binary factor (Shallow vs Deep). 3. Fit a linear mixed‐effects model: turnover ~ biomass + depth + (1|id_reef). 4. Examine coefficient for depth and its significance. 5. Check residuals for homoscedasticity and normality. 6. Visualize turnover vs biomass with separate depth lines.

Deliverables:
• Mixed‐effects model output with depth effect.  • Scatterplot of turnover vs biomass colored by depth with fitted lines.  • Residual diagnostic plots.

Analysis:
The linear mixed‐effects model (turnover ~ biomass + depth + (1|id_reef)) converged on 137,821 observations (245 reefs). Fixed‐effects estimates (REML):
  • Intercept (Deep baseline at biomass=0): 0.745 (95% CI 0.690 to 0.799), p < 0.001
  • C(depth)[T.Shallow]: +0.183 (95% CI 0.176 to 0.189), p < 0.001
  • biomass: –0.052 per t/ha (95% CI –0.057 to –0.047), p < 0.001
Random intercept variance (id_reef): 0.185.

Diagnostics reveal mild non‐normal residual tails and a negative biomass–turnover trend. The positive shallow coefficient indicates that, after accounting for biomass, shallow transects have significantly higher turnover than deep transects. Thus, the original hypothesis (deep > shallow turnover) is not supported by this model.

Hypothesis: Deep transects (20 m) exhibit higher biomass turnover rates than shallow transects (5 m), after controlling for biomass.

Implementation: A linear mixed‐effects model was fit to transect‐level data (137,821 observations) with turnover as the response, biomass and a depth factor (Deep baseline; Shallow dummy) as fixed effects, and a random intercept for reef (id_reef). Residual vs. fitted and Q–Q diagnostic plots were generated, along with a scatterplot of turnover vs. biomass colored by depth and overlaid with the model’s fitted lines.

Results: 
• Intercept (Deep at biomass = 0): 0.745 (95% CI 0.690–0.799, p < .001)
• Shallow vs. Deep: +0.183 (95% CI 0.176–0.189, p < .001)
• Biomass effect: –0.052 per t / ha (95% CI –0.057 to –0.047, p < .001)
• Random intercept variance (id_reef): 0.185

The positive Shallow coefficient indicates that, after accounting for biomass, shallow transects have significantly higher turnover than deep transects—i.e., deep transects exhibit lower turnover. The hypothesis (deep > shallow turnover) is therefore not supported. Residual diagnostics show mild non‐normal tails but no major heteroscedasticity. Overall, the experiment was implemented faithfully and the hypothesis was tested rigorously.

Experiment objective: Determine whether the slope of turnover ~ biomass changes between early and late study periods, indicating temporal shifts in community dynamics.

2. Compute turnover and biomass at transect level (or aggregate to reef‐year‐depth).
3. Fit a linear mixed‐effects model: turnover ~ biomass * period + (1|id_reef).
4. Examine the biomass × period interaction coefficient and its significance to test for slope change.
5. Perform model diagnostics and ensure no violation of homoscedasticity or normality.
6. Visualize turnover vs biomass scatterplots with separate regression lines for each period.

• Mixed‐model output showing biomass × period interaction estimate and p‐value.

{"code":"import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import statsmodels.api as sm

# 1. Load data and filter
df = pd.read_csv('reef.csv')
df = df[df['biomass'] > 0].copy()

# 2. Define period factor: Pre‐2010 vs Post‐2010
df['period'] = np.where(df['year'] <= 2010, 'Pre2010', 'Post2010')
df['period'] = df['period'].astype('category')

# 3. Fit mixed‐effects model: turnover ~ biomass * period + (1|id_reef)
model = smf.mixedlm('turnover ~ biomass * period', df, groups=df['id_reef'])
result = model.fit(reml=True)

# 4. Output model coefficients with CIs and p‐values
print("MixedLM Results:\n", result.summary())
intxn = result.params['biomass:period[T.Post2010]']
pval = result.pvalues['biomass:period[T.Post2010]']
ci = result.conf_int().loc['biomass:period[T.Post2010]'].tolist()
print(f"\nInteraction (biomass × Post2010): {intxn:.4f}, p-value = {pval:.4f}, 95% CI = [{ci[0]:.4f}, {ci[1]:.4f}]")

# 5. Diagnostics: residuals vs fitted and Q-Q
fitted = result.fittedvalues
resid = df['turnover'] - fitted
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
axes[0].scatter(fitted, resid, alpha=0.3)
axes[0].axhline(0, color='red', linestyle='--')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Fitted values')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Residuals')
axes[0].set_title('Residuals vs Fitted')
sm.qqplot(resid, line='45', ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title('Normal Q-Q')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 6. Scatterplot turnover vs biomass with period‐specific fitted lines
# Subsample for clarity
sub = df.sample(n=min(len(df), 5000), random_state=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
for per, grp in sub.groupby('period'):
    ax.scatter(grp['biomass'], grp['turnover'], label=per, alpha=0.3)
# Regression lines
biom_range = np.linspace(df['biomass'].min(), df['biomass'].max(), 100)
for per in df['period'].cat.categories:
    pred_df = pd.DataFrame({'biomass': biom_range, 'period': per})
    pred = result.predict(pred_df)
    ax.plot(biom_range, pred, linewidth=2, label=f'Fit {per}')
ax.set_xlabel('Biomass (t/ha)')
ax.set_ylabel('Turnover')
ax.set_title('Turnover vs Biomass by Period')
ax.legend()
plt.show()"}
